description: A timeline comparison of the GameStop blow-up vs. the broader short-squeeze battleground: GameStop (GME) and Melvin Capital’s flagship fund. We track the price/position shock from early 2021 through the post-squeeze unwind.

youtube_description:
🎬 GameStop didn’t just “spike”—it detonated. In this timeline chart-race, you’ll watch the market-cap explosion of GameStop (GME) alongside the blowback that hit one of the headline short-side players: Melvin Capital. 

📌 CHAPTERS
00:00 The moment the fuse lit (late 2020 → Q1 2021)
01:05 The gamma-squeeze surge (Jan–Mar 2021)
03:10 When the price peaked and reality broke (Q2 2021)
05:05 The unwind: what happened after the frenzy (Q3–Q4 2021)
06:55 The long hangover: 2022–2023 stabilization
08:20 The comeback/reshaping phase (2024)
10:00 2025: where the story lands now

🔥 What this video visualizes
• GameStop’s market-cap expansion from roughly single-digit billions into double-digit territory at the squeeze peak
• Melvin Capital’s reported catastrophic drawdown impact in early 2021, then the near-flat “survival-size” presence afterward as the firm restructured

✅ Watch until the end to see who “won” the timeline race: the meme-stock beta rocket vs. the short-squeeze casualties.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B GameStop Shockwave vs the short side that got wrecked.

In early 2021, GameStop (GME) went from a niche retail trade to the center of a global market panic. This wasn’t a slow climb—it was a combustion. In our timeline, GameStop starts around **$1.8B market cap (2020Q4)**, then rockets to **$8.2B (2021Q1)** as retail buying and options activity stacked pressure. By **2021Q2**, the squeeze environment turbocharged the move: GameStop hits **$23.5B**—the kind of leap that only happens when liquidity, leverage, and sentiment collide.

But the real drama is what the squeeze did to the short side. Melvin Capital—one of the most discussed names on the wrong end of the bet—shows the peak “damage” moment right when GameStop’s price action explodes. In **2021Q1**, Melvin’s reported drawdown impact hits **$14.0B**, then collapses to **$4.2B by 2021Q2**—a visual representation of how quickly a leveraged thesis can be forced to unwind when markets move against it.

After the peak, the chart becomes a story of two realities: retail momentum fades, and firms reassess risk. GameStop cools from **$23.5B (2021Q2)** down toward **$12.0B (2021Q3)** and **$7.3B (2021Q4)**, but it doesn’t fully disappear. Through **2022–2024**, it rebuilds its market-cap floor—rising into the high single digits and low double digits. By **2025Q4**, GameStop sits around **$21.0B**, suggesting the saga didn’t end with the squeeze—it transformed.

Meanwhile, the Melvin line essentially plateaus near **$0.4B impact** across later quarters, capturing the “survival-size” phase after the shock.

So here’s the question: 🧨 Do you think GameStop’s 2025 market-cap of **~$21.0B** is a true recovery—or just the next chapter of volatility? Drop your take below, then follow for more chart-race market stories.
facebook_caption:
GameStop’s “gamma squeeze” era reshaped market behavior in early 2021, and this timeline compares the rise of GameStop’s market-cap with the short-side damage attributed to Melvin Capital. 

GameStop begins around **$1.8B (2020Q4)** and accelerates to **$8.2B (2021Q1)** as retail participation and options positioning intensified. The squeeze conditions peak in **2021Q2**, when GameStop reaches **$23.5B**, before unwinding to **$12.0B (2021Q3)** and **$7.3B (2021Q4)**. Over 2022–2024, the market-cap stabilizes and rebuilds, reaching **$14.1B (2024Q4)** and approximately **$21.0B by 2025Q4**.

On the other side, Melvin Capital’s reported drawdown impact spikes in **2021Q1 at $14.0B**, then drops quickly as positions are forced to unwind—down to **$4.2B by 2021Q2**—followed by a much smaller, plateaued post-squeeze profile around **$0.4B** across later periods.

The takeaway: a market structure event can change both asset trajectories and fund survival outcomes—fast.
